correct_answer: The gap represents a genuine compliance deficiency — the regulation was effective March 1, 2024, Cascade's policy was updated to reflect the $3,000 threshold, but implementation was incomplete because the legacy Piedmont rule engine was not included in the system change; the institution's control environment failed to ensure the policy was operationalized across all platforms
rationale: The correct answer requires synthesizing information across all five systems. The regulation was effective March 1, 2024. Cascade's policy was updated (SharePoint v8 confirms the $3,000 threshold). The ServiceNow change was approved and implemented — but only for the primary rule engine. The critical signal hidden in the Outlook email reveals that the legacy Piedmont Bank rules (from the 2022 acquisition) ran on a separate instance that was never updated. This is a control gap: the institution had the right policy but failed to ensure it was operationalized across all systems. Answer A is wrong because the issue is not the 3-day delay (which WAS within tolerance) but the 9-month gap on the legacy platform — and a vendor defect defense fails because the institution owns its compliance program regardless of vendor responsibility. Answer B misreads the resolved comment — legal's 'prospective only' guidance meant they didn't need to re-run pre-March transactions, not that the new threshold could be delayed indefinitely for certain account segments. Answer B is incorrect because examination findings are not 'time-barred'; examiners can cite any deficiency that existed during the review period, and the gap persisted into the July-December 2024 review window.
